body:
WHAT
The version tool enforces Conventional Commits: a subject must read 'type(scope)!: subject'. checkMessage strips git comment lines, then reports problems for an empty message, a malformed header, a type not in version.config.json (11 types: feat, fix, perf, revert, docs, refactor, test, build, ci, chore, style), a scope not in the 10 configured scopes, an empty scope, a subject longer than 72 characters, a trailing full stop, a capitalised first word, a non-blank line right after the subject, and a BREAKING CHANGE footer with no text. Messages git writes itself ('Merge ...' and 'Revert "..."') are exempt.

WHY
The next version is computed from commit types (feat = minor, everything else = patch, '!' or a BREAKING CHANGE footer = major), so a message that does not parse would be dropped from the release and the changelog, or bump the wrong level.

WHERE
tools/version/lib/commits.mjs — HEADER regex, GIT_REVERT, isGitGenerated(subject), parseCommit(commit), hasBreakingFooter(body), checkMessage(message, config); configuration in version.config.json (types, scopes, subjectMaxLength) loaded by tools/version/lib/config.mjs loadConfig()/validateConfig().

TEST CHECKLIST
1. With the real config, checkMessage returns [] for every one of the 11 types used as '<type>: add thing' and for each of the 10 scopes as 'fix(<scope>): add thing'; 'wip: x' yields a problem 'Unknown type: "wip"' listing the allowed types and 'fix(web): x' yields 'Unknown scope: "web"'.
2. A subject of exactly 72 characters passes and one of 73 characters yields a problem stating the length and the maximum 72.
3. 'Merge branch \'x\' into main' and 'Revert "feat: thing"' return [] even though neither matches HEADER, while 'Reverting stuff' does not qualify and is reported as malformed.
4. 'feat: Add thing.' reports both 'ends with a full stop' and 'starts with a capital letter'; 'feat: x\nbody' reports the non-empty line after the subject; 'feat: x\n\nBREAKING CHANGE:' reports the footer with no description; and lines starting with '#' are ignored so a git-template message still checks its real subject.
5. parseCommit({subject:'feat(core)!: x'}).breaking is true, parseCommit({subject:'fix: x', body:'BREAKING-CHANGE: y'}).breaking is true, parseCommit({subject:'fix: x', body:'BREAKING CHANGE'}).breaking is false, and parseCommit({subject:'nonsense'}) is null.
